summaries.example: Imagine a drawing of a cat. The drawing is flat, but its shapes and colors may help you recognize a cat. A philosopher who favors resemblance might say the drawing works partly because some of its visible features are like features of cats. Another philosopher might say that art uses learned picture-making practices. A third might focus on what happens in your mind when you look at the drawing: you may see a cat in the marks and imagine that you are looking at one.
summaries.summary: Depiction is the philosophical study of how pictures represent things. One traditional idea says that a picture represents an object because some of its shapes and colors resemble the object’s visible features. This idea is appealing, but it faces puzzles. A picture does not usually represent itself, even though it resembles itself, and a copy may resemble the original picture more closely than it resembles the object shown. Pictures can also show imaginary characters or kinds of things, such as a unicorn or a horse, without showing one particular existing object. Philosophers have therefore developed more careful resemblance theories. Some focus on viewpoint and the shapes that objects present to an observer. Others allow different kinds of visible resemblance and give a role to the maker’s intention. Critics propose alternatives. Conventionalist theories stress learned systems and rules. Experiential theories focus on what viewers experience, such as seeing a subject in a surface or imagining it in a game of make-believe. Recognition-based theories focus on the abilities that let viewers identify what a picture shows. The entry also examines realism. It distinguishes realistic subject matter, such as ordinary daily life, from realistic technique, such as ways of showing space, light, movement, or materials. No single simple test settles every case, especially because pictures come in many styles.
key_ideas: Some philosophers explain pictures partly through resemblance: visible features of a picture may be like features of what it shows.
Simple resemblance is not enough. A picture can look more like another picture than like its subject, and a picture may show something imaginary or a whole kind of thing.
Other theories say that picture-making depends on learned conventions, what viewers experience, or their ability to recognize things.
Realism can mean choosing everyday subjects, using lifelike techniques, or expanding what an artistic style can show. These are different ideas.
summaries.why_it_matters: Pictures are everywhere: in books, maps, photographs, screens, and art. Understanding depiction helps us ask how an image can communicate without being a sentence. It also helps us notice that seeing a picture is not always just copying the world. What we know, what we expect, artistic customs, and the picture’s design may all matter.

important_terms.definition: A picture or other image that shows, presents, or stands for something.
Being alike in some way, such as having similar shapes, colors, or patterns.
A shared way of using signs or images that people learn and understand together.
The idea that a picture can make us notice one thing in its marks while still noticing the surface itself.
How much an artwork seems true to life. Philosophers disagree about what makes an artwork realistic.

questions_to_think_about: Can a picture show something that does not exist? What would it resemble?
If two drawings use different styles, can both show the same animal?
When you look at a picture, do you notice the marks, the subject, or both at once?
What might make one picture seem more realistic than another?

summaries.example: Consider a portrait of a person seated in a room. It may resemble the person in visible shape and color, but that does not by itself explain why it represents that individual: the portrait may resemble other people or even another portrait more closely. A resemblance theorist might distinguish the picture’s sense, or way of presenting its subject, from its reference, or whom it represents. A conventionalist might explain its reference through a pictorial symbol system. An experiential theorist might analyze the viewer’s simultaneous awareness of the surface and the represented scene. summaries.summary: The philosophy of depiction asks how pictures represent objects, people, scenes, kinds, and fictional entities. Resemblance theories begin with the thought that pictorial representation differs from linguistic representation because pictures resemble what they represent. Yet bare resemblance cannot be sufficient: it is reflexive and symmetric, whereas depiction is generally neither; copies may resemble pictures more than their subjects; and generic or fictional depiction raises questions about what the picture could resemble. These objections do not automatically eliminate resemblance. They may show only that resemblance explains the pictorial character, or sense, of a representation rather than its reference. Recent proposals refine the relevant resemblance through viewpoint-relative optical properties, or allow different visible respects of resemblance selected partly by the maker’s communicative intentions. Such theories must address diversity across artistic styles and the independence constraint, according to which viewers should be able to perceive the relevant resemblance without already knowing the subject. Conventionalist theories reject resemblance as the fundamental explanation. Goodman treats depiction as denotation in a symbol system and characterizes pictorial systems by structural features such as density and repleteness. His account, however, faces disputes about digital images, diagrams, portraits, fictional subjects, natural generativity, and the lack of clearly specified pictorial rules. Experiential theories instead examine seeing-in, experienced resemblance, or visual make-believe; recognition-based theories emphasize the activation of recognitional abilities. key_ideas: The formula 'a picture depicts whatever it resembles' fails because resemblance is normally reflexive and symmetric, while depiction is not. It also cannot by itself explain fictional subjects, generic depiction, or the role of context and intention.

A more sophisticated resemblance approach may explain pictorial sense rather than reference. Hyman connects surface marks with viewpoint-relative optical properties, while Abell allows different visible respects of resemblance shaped by communicative intentions.

Goodman’s conventionalism treats depiction as denotation within a symbol system rather than as representation explained by resemblance. His account describes pictorial systems as analog, dense, and relatively replete, but each claim has been challenged.

Experiential accounts analyze what viewing a picture is like. Wollheim’s 'twofoldness' joins awareness of surface and content; other accounts appeal to experienced resemblance or visual make-believe. Critics question whether these approaches explain how surface marks constrain content.

Recognition-based theories stress natural generativity: once viewers can interpret some pictures and recognize the depicted objects, they may interpret new pictures without being given a separate convention for each one. Critics ask what explains the recognition link.

Realism is not one thing. Subject-matter realism concerns the kinds of subjects and treatment chosen; technical realism concerns capacities for representing information, movement, materials, space, light, and other features.
summaries.why_it_matters: Theories of depiction affect how we understand photographs, paintings, diagrams, illustrations, and digital images. They clarify why a picture can communicate without functioning exactly like a sentence, why style and viewer training matter, and why a picture may show more or less than it visibly resembles. The debate also separates several questions that are often run together: what a picture refers to, how it presents its subject, what viewers experience, and what makes one style realistic.

important_terms.definition: A theory that gives resemblance between a picture and what it depicts an important role in explaining pictorial representation.
A relation of reference: what a representation stands for or picks out.
A way an object is presented or understood, distinct from the object to which the presentation refers.
A shared system of signs, practices, or rules that helps determine how representations are understood.
A visual experience in which awareness of a picture’s surface and awareness of something represented are connected.
A proposed ability of pictures to prompt recognition of the kinds of objects they depict.
The requirement that relevant resemblances should be perceptible without the viewer first knowing what the picture represents.
The broad issue of what makes art realistic; the entry separates realistic subject matter from realistic technique.

questions_to_think_about: Does resemblance explain pictorial reference, pictorial sense, or both?
Can a theory of depiction explain a picture of a fictional character or a generic picture of a horse?
Are pictorial conventions fundamentally like linguistic conventions, or does natural recognition make pictures different?
Can viewers be aware of both a picture’s surface and its content in one experience?
If realism depends partly on visual habits, can a new style still become more realistic for its viewers?

summaries.example: Suppose you see a simple drawing of a skateboarder. The drawing may use a few lines that resemble a body, wheels, and motion. But resemblance alone cannot settle what the drawing represents. The same lines could be copied in another picture, and that copy might look more like the first drawing than like a real skateboarder. You also need to ask about the drawing’s style, the artist’s purpose, what viewers can recognize, and what they experience while looking at it. Different philosophical theories give different answers.
summaries.summary: Depiction means pictorial representation: the way a picture shows or stands for something. A traditional approach begins with resemblance. A portrait seems to represent its subject partly because its shapes and colors are like the subject’s visible appearance. But philosophers point out that resemblance behaves differently from representation. An object resembles itself, yet it does not normally represent itself; a picture may resemble another picture more closely than its subject; and some pictures show fictional individuals or general kinds rather than particular existing objects. These points make a simple resemblance definition inadequate, though they do not prove that every resemblance-based theory must fail. More developed versions try to specify the relevant visible features, the viewer’s point of view, and the artist’s communicative intentions. Goodman offers a contrasting conventionalist theory. He treats depiction as a type of denotation within a symbol system and argues that pictorial systems differ from language in features such as density and repleteness. Critics challenge whether this explains portraits, digital pictures, diagrams, and the ability to understand new pictures naturally. Experiential theories focus on the viewer. Wollheim describes 'seeing-in' as a distinctive experience involving both surface and content; other theories appeal to experienced resemblance or visual make-believe. Recognition-based theories emphasize the skills that let viewers identify depicted objects, but they still need to explain why particular marks activate those skills. Finally, the entry discusses realism. key_ideas: The resemblance view is a useful starting point, but the quick rule 'a picture depicts whatever it resembles' is too simple.
Pictures can represent imaginary individuals and general kinds, so a theory must explain more than portraits of existing people.
Goodman argues that resemblance does not explain depiction. He says pictures, like words, work through symbol systems, although pictorial systems have distinctive structural features.
Experiential theories focus on the viewer’s response, including seeing-in, experienced resemblance, and imagining in a game of make-believe.
Recognition-based theories say pictures work by activating abilities that help viewers identify objects. Critics ask what explains the connection between marks and recognition.
The entry separates realism in subject matter from realism in technique and questions whether realism is just familiarity with a customary style.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about depiction helps explain why images can communicate even when they contain no words. It also shows why interpretation depends on more than simple visual copying. Artists’ intentions, viewers’ abilities, conventions, styles, and the structure of an image may all play different roles. The topic is useful for understanding art, photographs, diagrams, film images, and digital pictures.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical question of how an image shows or stands for something else.
A likeness between things in one or more respects, such as shape or color.
A learned practice or shared rule that helps people understand a sign or image.
The relation in which a representation stands for what it represents.
The experience of noticing both a picture’s physical surface and something represented in that surface.
The idea that pictures can lead viewers to identify the kinds of objects they show.
The condition that a viewer should be able to notice relevant resemblance without first being told the subject.
A quality often associated with lifelike art, though philosophers distinguish realistic subjects from realistic methods.

questions_to_think_about: Why is resemblance not enough to explain why a picture represents one thing rather than another?
Would a picture of a unicorn need to resemble a real unicorn?
How might a viewer’s experience help explain depiction?
Are pictures more like words, more like objects, or different from both?
What is the difference between showing ordinary life and using lifelike artistic techniques?
